title: Dispatches from Harvard 2026
author: Sylvia Duarte
summary: In a guest post for Eric Wearne's Restarting School, Sylvia Duarte reports from the fifth Emerging School Models Conference at Harvard's Kennedy School, where the new federal Education Freedom Tax Credit dominated nearly every session. She explains the mechanics: taxpayers can redirect up to $1,700 of federal liability to certified scholarship granting organizations funding tuition, tutoring and other expenses for families up to 300 percent of area median income, with 30 governors opted in and estimates of 30 to 60 billion dollars a year. Her central question for hybrid schools and microschools is what counts as a school, since states will write that definition and many hybrid families are legally homeschoolers. She sets out Assistant Secretary Kirsten Baesler's plea for broad, simple definitions that expand rather than recreate existing models, the NEA's objection that public dollars belong in public schools, and Governor Jared Polis's bipartisan case for opting in. She closes with a practical call for unconventional school leaders to engage state legislatures now, while SGO certification is still being set up and before a future Congress can roll the program back.
points: Duarte identifies the statutory word school as the hinge on which hybrid schools and microschools will win or lose access to the new tax credit.
Baesler warned that narrow state definitions would simply recreate familiar models, undercutting a program meant to expand them.
An audience member cautioned that once a state labels a homeschool group a school for tax-credit purposes, the label may stick for regulation too.
Polis framed the credit as extending tutoring and enrichment advantages of wealthy families across the income spectrum, including teachers as likely tutors.
The report urges school founders to track state SGO certification and shape definitions now because the window could close under a future Congress.
quotes: For anyone running, launching or otherwise engaged with a hybrid school or other unconventional model, the central question is, what counts as a “school?
Even on the conservative end, that represents a roughly 50% increase in federal-level education spending - but directed by individual taxpayers.
For innovative models like hybrids that don’t look like conventional schools under existing law, everything hinges on how broadly legislatures write that definition.

Legislators or states should not be defining these things so narrowly that we’re just re-creating the same models we’ve always had. This is meant to expand the models. I fear that the tendencies will be to re-create what is normal and comfortable.
They will begin to define a school more broadly, and suddenly a school defined as a school only for this will become a school for everything else as well.

Basically, what you’re doing here is you’re making sure every kid has the same advantage as a family making half a million or a million dollars a year. Guess what, they can afford a tutor, they can afford summer camp.
What we’re looking at could be transformational for innovative school models, but only if the people who run them engage at the state level now to shape definitions
